newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour may turn to backdoor taxes-analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour may turn to backdoor taxes-analysts.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party pledged this week not to raise income taxes if it wins power, but analysts said the party can simply turn to backdoor taxes if it wants to spend more.
"There are plenty of ways for an incoming Labour government to raise revenue without changing income tax rates," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.
With over 200 tax exemptions, reliefs and allowances in the tax system to choose from, the party still has huge room for fiscal manoeuvre despite the tax promise.

Labour also surprised markets by pledging to stick to public spending targets set by the Conservative government for the first two years of the next five-year parliament -- a clear effort to demonstrate how fiscally frugal the party has become.
Finance spokesman Gordon Brown said Labour wanted to send the "clearest possible signal that we want to encourage employment and reward work, not penalise it."

British voters have been mesmerised for decades by the main rates of income tax, and applauded sharp cuts delivered by Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, particularly in 1988 when the top rate of tax crashed to 40 percent from 60 percent at a stroke.
But the Conservatives, in power since 1979, have relied heavily on backdoor tax increases -- such as restricting the value of tax allowances -- to raise revenue.

Labour's growing political sophistication appears to have led the party up the same tactical path to the conclusion that that no party wins elections promising higher taxes, even for the super-rich. "The Conservatives raised 17 billion pounds ($28 billion) in 1993 budgets without touching the main rates of income tax once," said Chris Giles, economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies.
Those tax rises, as Labour has argued, were equivalent to putting over seven pence on the basic rate of income tax.
So while on the face of it Labour may have made a historic break with its tax-and-spend past, analysts said the move may be more symbolic than real.
The party will still be able to embrace a more redistributive and progressive tax system, but much less aggressively than in the 1970s or 1960s.
"Labour are clearly aiming for at least two terms in office," said Lyons of DKB.
"The party is producing a programme first to woo the floating voter, woo the financial markets, and then, further down the line, woo the traditional Labour supporter."
"It is a patient programme which asks party activists who have waited 18 years for a change of government to wait for a further two before they see the rewards."
In power, Labour would be spoilt for choice on tax-raising measures.
It could scrap tax relief on mortgage interest payments (raising 2.4 billion pounds), the married couples' allowance (2.8 billion) or the tax credit on advance corporation tax (5.0 billion).

But, significantly, Labour's tax pledges mean it will not be able to "squeeze the rich until the pips squeak," as Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer Dennis Healey promised during the last Labour government in the 1970s.
The top rate of income tax will stay at 40 percent and fiddling with tax allowances does not significantly affect the incomes of very high earners.

Real blood may be spilt, however, in the forthcoming public spending round if Labour wins power, with the party forced to take an ultra-tough line against Whitehall departments which will be pushing for extra money from the new government.

The spending targets set by the government over the next two fiscal years are far tougher than those achieved since the 1992 election, and an incoming Labour government with pledges on health and education may be in for a rough ride, not least from its traditional bugbear -- strong public sector unions, which have a loyal following among many Labour rank-and-file members.
"Labour wants to examine departmental spending but in truth this will have to involve cuts in services," warns Giles of the IFS. "The public spending round could get nasty."
Many think the tough spending targets will not be met, and money will have to be found to balance the books.
"The markets are taking promises from both parties to hit spending targets with a pinch of salt," said Jeremy Hawkins, economist at Bank America.
